assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks are a textbook case of a new measurement technique opening new physics: magic-wavelength trapping removes Doppler and recoil shifts while interrogating huge numbers of atoms, giving fractional uncertainties near 1e-18. They underpin tests of fundamental constants, relativistic geodesy and a possible redefinition of the second. Impact reaches well beyond atomic physics.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and demonstrated early strontium clocks; Ye built the leading Sr clocks and pushed systematic uncertainty and coherence to the extreme. A two-person prize is clean. Related ion-clock and comb work is already recognized (Hall, Hansch, Wineland), and I am not certain how the committee would weigh other lattice-clock contributors, so the two-name configuration is my best reading.
assessment.maturity: Multiple independent groups (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE and others) have confirmed and surpassed the original performance, and clock comparisons are routine. Recognition is timely and the field is mature, with the redefinition of the second still pending.
uncertainties: Whether the committee views this as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes on combs and ion control.
I cannot independently verify the latest uncertainty figures cited for the leading clocks.
Other credited contributors, for example early lattice-clock theory, may be argued to merit inclusion.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Atom interferometry turned matter-wave coherence into a precision instrument, measuring gravity, rotation, the fine-structure constant and testing the equivalence principle. As a measurement method it has opened gravimetry, inertial navigation and fundamental tests, and large-scale instruments are now planned. The conceptual originality and the breadth of use are both high.
assessment.attribution: Pritchard realized early atom interferometers and atom optics, Bordé provided the key theoretical and Ramsey-Bordé interferometer framework, and Kasevich made the high-sensitivity gravimeters and gradiometers and the long-baseline devices. Together these three give a coherent configuration. Holger Mueller's later precision measurements are significant but I judge his contribution more derivative, and I also note that Chu, Cohen-Tannoudji and Phillips were recognized earlier for cooling.
assessment.maturity: Experimental demonstration is strong and replicated across many labs, with commercial and field-deployed devices. Sensitivity records are still moving and large-scale tests are in progress, so recognition is mature but the headline fundamental result is still to come.
uncertainties: Division of credit between the Bordé theory, Pritchard's Ramsey-type interferometers and Kasevich's sensor work is debatable.
The fine-structure-constant and equivalence-principle results rely on continuing systematic-error control that I cannot verify here.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED created the standard architecture for superconducting qubits: strong coupling of an artificial atom to a microwave resonator, dispersive readout and two-qubit gates. It is the experimental basis of today's superconducting quantum processors and linked quantum optics and solid-state circuits. The idea is original and the lasting impact is very large.
assessment.attribution: Blais, Huang, Wallraff, Girvin and Schoelkopf wrote the 2004 proposal and Wallraff, Schoelkopf and colleagues did the first strong-coupling experiment. Girvin is a close contributor but the three-name limit makes the choice delicate. I selected the two leading experimentalists plus Blais as the lead theorist, while noting that this is a judgement call.
assessment.maturity: Independently confirmed by many groups and widely commercialized. However, the 2025 prize recognized macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits, so a further circuit-based prize this soon would need distinct justification.
uncertainties: Possible committee reluctance to follow the 2025 superconducting-circuit prize so closely.
Unresolved credit between Girvin, Blais and the experimentalists.
Whether the practical device payoff is considered separate from the underlying physics.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Squeezed light beats the standard quantum limit in interferometry, and its routine use in gravitational-wave detectors is a measurement advance with direct scientific consequences. The idea is fundamental quantum optics (Caves) and the experimental realization required years of work on losses and noise.
assessment.attribution: Caves supplied the theory of squeezed-state interferometry, Kimble produced early experimental squeezing and Schnabel contributed to the realization in GEO600 and LIGO. Slusher, Wu and others made the first squeezed-light demonstrations, and Mavalvala and the LIGO squeezing team were decisive for LIGO. Credit allocation is the main weakness, so the selection of three names is uncertain.
assessment.maturity: Squeezing is now operational in LIGO, Virgo and GEO600 and has been confirmed repeatedly. The impact is real, but the fundamental advance is partly an enabling technology for a field that has already received a prize (2017).
uncertainties: Credit is spread across theory, first experiments and detector integration.
I cannot verify the relative roles of the instrument teams versus the credited individuals.
Possible view that this is an enhancement of an already recognized discovery.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Aberration-corrected electron microscopy broke the spherical-aberration limit and provided routine sub-angstrom imaging of atoms. It is a new measurement capability with enormous reach across materials, nanoscience and condensed matter, and is a very concrete experimental instrument advance.
assessment.attribution: Rose proposed the correctors, Haider and Urban built and demonstrated working systems, and Krivanek is a notable and, in this list, absent contributor. The three credited names form a natural and well-documented configuration, although the omission of Krivanek and others raises fairness concerns.
assessment.maturity: Fully mature, with commercial instruments installed worldwide and decades of independent use. Recognition is overdue rather than premature, but it may be viewed as chemistry or materials science rather than physics.
uncertainties: Disciplinary fit: the committee may view electron microscopy as outside physics proper.
Omitted contributors, such as the Krivanek group, are not available in the credited list.
Past recognition of electron-microscope work (Ruska, 1986) may affect appetite.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical readout and coherent control of single defect spins in diamond opened nanoscale quantum sensing, biological and materials magnetometry, and entanglement-based quantum networks, all at room temperature or with modest cooling. It matches my interest in quantum sensors and shows long coherence times and practical sensitivity.
assessment.attribution: Wrachtrup demonstrated single NV optical detection of magnetic resonance, Awschalom developed spin control and defect engineering across materials, and Hanson achieved the remote entanglement and loophole-free work. Lukin and Walsworth contributed to sensing and registers, and five credited names exceed the three-laureate limit, so any selection leaves out significant contributors.
assessment.maturity: Many groups have confirmed the core results, but sensing applications are still developing and the maturity differs between the sensing and networking parts. The compound nature of the topic could lead to a premature or fragmented award.
uncertainties: A compound discovery in which sensing and networking might need different recognition.
The limit of three laureates leaves out Lukin and Walsworth.
Whether practical sensing advantages are demonstrated beyond lab settings.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Rydberg-blockade neutral-atom arrays with optical tweezers enable programmable quantum simulation and gate operations with hundreds of atoms. This is a rapidly advancing platform with high-profile demonstrations of many-body physics and error-corrected logical operations.
assessment.attribution: Lukin, Browaeys and Saffman contributed key proposals and demonstrations of blockade and tweezer arrays. Other contributors, for example Jaksch and Zoller (gate proposals) and Bloch, Ahn, Lahaye and Weiss, are not all in this credited list, so the attribution seems incomplete.
assessment.maturity: Field is moving quickly and results are being confirmed by multiple groups, but the long-term stable interpretation and impact are not fully settled. The recognition may be somewhat premature compared with the other candidates I rank higher.
uncertainties: Possible prematurity given the rapid evolution of the platform.
Credit overlap with the Hubbard simulation and trapped-ion theory candidates.
Claims of fault tolerance are recent and I cannot independently verify them.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Coherent light-matter interfaces, including EIT and slow light, quantum memories and single-atom cavity QED, are the building blocks of quantum networks and repeaters. The concept of storing and retrieving photonic states with high efficiency is fundamental. I know this area closely and have to apply a high bar for experimental demonstration given its long road from proof of principle to repeater use.
assessment.attribution: Lukin, Kimble and Rempe each made decisive contributions to coherent light-matter interaction, but the topic mixes atomic ensembles, single atoms in cavities and solid-state memories, so the boundary is unclear. I declare my own field's proximity, and other groups, including rare-earth-crystal work, are not credited here.
assessment.maturity: Individual experiments are well reproduced, but a functioning scalable quantum network has not yet been built, so the whole is not yet mature. Basic elements are established, while the application impact is still emerging.
uncertainties: A compound topic that spans several different physical systems.
Practical efficiency, storage time and repeater performance remain limiting.
My own research proximity may bias my view, which I note for transparency.
